content.title: About
content.content: Vegetables are edible parts of plants such as roots, leaves, stems, and fruits that are commonly used in stews to add flavor, aroma, and nutritional value. Typical stew vegetables include carrots, onions, celery, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, and zucchini.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables form the base of many traditional dishes worldwide, such as French "bouillon" and Italian "minestrone".
Their variety of colors and textures makes them ideal for creating visually appealing stews.
Aromatics like onion and garlic release sulfur compounds that enhance the overall scent of the dish.
Seasonal vegetables often have brighter flavors and higher vitamin content than out‑of‑season imports.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as potassium, magnesium, and folate, supporting immune function and heart health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Vegetables increase the volume of a stew without adding many calories, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Pigments like carotenoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports gut health
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in certain vegetables foster the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific vegetables such as tomatoes or peppers.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Improperly washed vegetables can retain pesticide residues; thorough rinsing or choosing organic produce is recommended.

items.title: Oxalate overload
items.content: Vegetables high in oxalates, like spinach and beetroot, may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Vegetables are usually diced or sliced and sautéed briefly in a little oil until softened, then combined with broth, meat or legumes and simmered over low heat. For deeper flavor add tomato paste, herbs (thyme, rosemary) and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer in perforated bags. Root vegetables (carrots, potatoes) keep best in a cool, dark place. Cooked vegetable mixtures should be kept in an airtight container for 3‑4 days.
